name: Dahlia Carmine
lede: Dahlia Carmine is a dark, muted purplish red named for carmine, the red dye made from cochineal insects, and recorded by Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A dye-insect's name
sections.body: The nearest named colors on file are [[corinthian-purple]], [[dark-vinaceous-purple]], [[perilla-purple]] and [[purple-brown]], at 3.9, 4, 4.2 and 4.6 ΔE [1]. Ridgway's 1912 standards place it on plate XXVI, hue 71′, tone k, Maerz and Paul separately date a close match to 1912 on plate 46 L 3 of their 1930 dictionary, and the 2010 xkcd color survey carries a near-duplicate under the name Brownish Purple, only 0.7 units of ΔE away [1]. In LCH terms it is dark and moderately saturated: lightness 34, chroma 25, hue 6 degrees [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a close match to Dahlia Carmine in 37, about 0.2 percent, as photographed [2]. Its earliest appearance, a Roman-period portrait the archive dates to about 100, is the same picture that carries the earliest match to [[copper-rose]], a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. Its heaviest use, relative to his own baseline, falls to Henri Matisse, nearly 39 times expected, and the archive's use of it peaks in the 1910s, in 5 of 523 paintings [2].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature; ColorHub library

questions.q: Carmine, the dye Dahlia Carmine is named for, comes from what source?
True or false: carmine and madder are made from the same source.

openers: Dahlia Carmine's earliest archive match shares a single Roman-period portrait with Copper Rose.

issues: Field notes claimed the earliest Dahlia Carmine match was also the earliest match for Copper Penny; the archive's earliest Copper Penny match is a different painting (aic-14968, c. 500), not the Roman-period portrait (nga-43626, c. 100) shared with Copper Rose. Removed the incorrect Copper Penny claim.
